strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated question — what is the minimal optimizer state needed for Adam-level LLM pretraining performance — and pursues it with a genuinely systematic, bottom-up ablation (Table 2: normalization variants; Table 3: normalization + last-layer momentum; Figure 3: layer-wise gradient variance), rather than proposing an ad hoc combination.

The resulting optimizer (SCALE) is extremely simple (column-wise normalization + momentum only on the LM head), requires near-SGD memory (13.74GB vs 13.48GB for SGD on 7B), and the empirical evidence is reasonably broad: LLaMA 60M–1B plus a 7B run where SCALE beats APOLLO(-Mini) in both perplexity (12.59 vs 13.02/13.09) and memory (13.74G vs 16.14G/14.53G).

The steepest-descent/trust-region framing (Eq. 2.6–2.7, building on Bernstein & Newhouse 2024 and Pethick et al. 2025) neatly unifies sign, row-, column-, and singular-value normalization, and Table 1 quantifying compute costs of each normalization is a useful practical contribution.

Theorem 2.1 provides a (standard but relevant) convergence analysis for layer-wise momentum hyperparameters, and Remark 2.1 connects it to the design choice of applying momentum only where gradient variance is large; the variance measurements in Figure 3 empirically support the last-layer choice.
Connections and differences to prior work (Muon, SWAN, SCION, APOLLO) are explicitly discussed (Table 4), and memory accounting is transparently detailed in Appendix A.1.
weaknesses: Originality is modest: both ingredients already exist — column-wise normalization appears in Pethick et al. (2025) and SWAN uses Adam on first/last layers; the contribution is essentially a careful ablation identifying a low-memory subset of known components. This is useful but incremental.

Several headline baselines are copied from other papers rather than re-run under identical conditions (SWAN from Ma et al. 2024; Adam/Stable-SPAM/GaLore/Fira from Glentis et al. 2025; APOLLO at 7B from Zhu et al. 2025). Cross-paper comparisons are vulnerable to setup mismatch, and some of these sources themselves differ in sequence length and token budget.

The 7B experiment is thin: a single run at a single learning rate (1e-4, explicitly stated as untuned), compared only against APOLLO(-Mini) and not against Adam, Muon, or Stable-SPAM. The claim of outperforming 'state-of-the-art' at 7B is therefore weakly supported; at 1B, SCALE (14.25) actually loses to APOLLO-Mini (14.13), Stable-SPAM, and Muon.

The experimental regime is small-scale in an important sense: sequence length 256, batch size 512, and up to 19.7B tokens. Optimizer rankings are known to shift with scale and longer contexts, so transfer to realistic pretraining setups is unverified.

The theory is loosely coupled to the actual algorithm: Theorem 2.1 analyzes plain SGD-M without normalization, and the authors explicitly decline to give a convergence proof for Algorithm 1; the gap between the analyzed object and SCALE weakens the theoretical justification of the design.

The gradient-variance methodology (using a 512-sample batch as a proxy for the true gradient) is approximate and validated only on the 130M model; the claim that the last layer dominates gradient variance may not hold across scales or architectures.

Presentation issues: several typos ('vanila', 'signular-value', 'highly-performed', a stray parenthesis in Remark 2.1), inconsistent notation in Algorithm 1 (last-layer momentum is written with a single sample ξ_t while g_t is the batch mean), and no explicit statement about releasing code, which matters for a paper whose pitch is a minimalist community baseline.
The memory figures exclude activations and other training overheads, so the practical end-to-end memory advantage (e.g., vs SWAN at 14.52G) is smaller than the table suggests.

strengths: The bottom-up, minimalist framing is a genuinely useful contribution: systematically decomposing Adam into gradient normalization vs. EMA (Section 2) and ablating four normalization families (Table 2) with last-layer momentum (Table 3) provides a cleaner evidence trail than most optimizer papers.

The layer-wise gradient variance analysis (Figure 3) gives a concrete, checkable empirical motivation for restricting momentum to the last layer, rather than presenting SCALE as an unexplained combination of tricks.

Honest positioning relative to prior work: the connections to SCION/Pethick et al. (2025), SWAN, and Muon are discussed explicitly (Section 3, Table 4), and the authors candidly note that the convergence argument for Algorithm 1 would not explain why the components help.
Memory accounting is transparent and reproducible from the parameter counts given in Appendix A.1, and the learning-rate sensitivity study (Appendix A.4) is a useful robustness check.
SCALE is simple (a few lines on top of SGD), so the practical artifact is easy to audit and reimplement.
weaknesses: The central empirical claim is weaker than stated. In Table 5, SCALE trails Stable-SPAM and Muon at 60M (30.81 vs 28.77/28.86), 130M (22.57 vs 22.20/22.20), and 1B (14.25 vs 13.97/14.18); it only wins at 350M. Framing this as 'matching or exceeding' Adam and 'competitive with Muon' overstates the evidence, and the claim to be a 'strong candidate for large-scale pretraining' is not supported at the scales where it loses.

The 7B experiment (Table 6) compares only against APOLLO(-Mini), with results copied from Zhu et al. (2025), and uses a single untuned learning rate (1e-4). There is no Adam, Muon, or Stable-SPAM comparison at 7B, so the abstract's headline 7B claim rests on one baseline taken from another paper under possibly different training conditions.

Mixed provenance of baseline numbers undermines comparability: Adam/Stable-SPAM/GaLore/Fira come from Glentis et al. (2025), SWAN from Ma et al. (2024) (code unavailable), while SCALE runs were tuned via the authors' own wandb sweeps. Different tuning budgets across methods make the Pareto-frontier claim (Figure 1) hard to assess.

The theory does not analyze the proposed method. Theorem 2.1 covers layer-wise-momentum SGD without normalization, and its per-layer momentum conclusion (Remark 2.1) is heuristic (e.g., the statement that β_l = 1−δ is 'optimal' contradicts the memory-driven choice β_l = 0 for all but the last layer). The design of SCALE is therefore supported by ablations, not by the theoretical component.

Training budgets are small (1.4B–13.1B tokens, sequence length 256), a regime known to reward different optimizers than longer-horizon training; there is no evidence the last-layer variance phenomenon (Figure 3, measured only on 130M) persists at scale or across architectures/tokenizations.

Adafactor — the natural same-memory baseline with O(d) state — appears in Table 4 but is absent from the main perplexity comparisons (Tables 5–6), even though its memory cost is essentially identical to SCALE's.
No code release is mentioned anywhere in the manuscript, which is a significant reproducibility gap for a paper whose contribution is an empirical optimizer design.

The writing has multiple typos and rough edges ('vanila SGD', 'signular-value', 'highly-performed', a stray parenthesis in Remark 2.1), and A.3 (perplexity curves) and A.4 are placed before their content, suggesting an unfinished polish pass.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated question — identifying the minimal optimizer state needed for Adam-level LLM pretraining performance — through a clean, systematic bottom-up ablation of gradient normalization types (Table 2) and momentum placement (Figure 3, Table 3), which is more principled than the typical 'combine many tricks' approach in this literature.

The proposed SCALE optimizer is extremely simple (column-wise normalization plus momentum only on the last layer), easy to implement, and the empirical evidence is reasonably broad: LLaMA 60M–1B with hyperparameter sweeps, plus a 7B run showing SCALE (13.74G) beating APOLLO (13.02 vs 12.59 perplexity at 150K steps) with less memory.

The paper honestly situates its contribution relative to prior work (SCION, SWAN, Adafactor), provides a transparent accounting of the memory of each method in Appendix A.1, and transparently notes when results are copied from prior benchmarks (Glentis et al., Ma et al.) and when replication failed (SWAN).

The layer-wise gradient variance analysis (Figure 3) gives an empirical justification for placing momentum only in the last layer, and the convergence analysis in Theorem 2.1 (with full proof in Appendix A.5) provides qualitative support for the variance-dependent momentum design.
weaknesses: Overclaiming in the abstract and text: the claim that SCALE 'consistently outperforms memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore, Fira and APOLLO' is contradicted by Table 5 at the 1B scale, where APOLLO (14.20) and APOLLO-Mini (14.13) both achieve better perplexity than SCALE (14.25), albeit with slightly more memory. The result is better described as Pareto-competitive, not uniformly dominant.

The reported 1B SCALE result (14.25) depends on adopting Muon's learning-rate scaling trick (Appendix A.2); without it the result is 14.34, which is behind Muon (14.18) and closer to the baselines, which weakens the headline 'matches or exceeds' claim at the largest scale tested with full sweeps.

The theory does not analyze the proposed algorithm: Theorem 2.1 covers per-layer-momentum SGD-M without normalization, and the authors explicitly decline to prove convergence for Algorithm 1 (Section 3). Remark 2.1's argument connecting the bound to the last-layer design is qualitative; the key empirical premise (last layer has highest variance) rests on a single 130M run using a 512-batch proxy for the full gradient and only visualizes the first and last layers.

The 7B comparison is thin: a single run with a single learning rate (1e-4), only against APOLLO/APOLLO-Mini (copied from Zhu et al.), and SCALE is behind at 40K/80K steps, only ahead at 120K/150K. No Adam, Muon, or Stable-SPAM 7B baselines were run, so 'state-of-the-art' claims at 7B rest on a narrow comparison.

Limited novelty: column-wise normalization with per-layer normalization choices is already present in Pethick et al. (2025), and selective treatment of first/last layers appears in SWAN, GaLore, etc.; the contribution is essentially a careful minimal combination of known components, supported by good ablations but a somewhat incremental method.

Experimental setup is dated for pretraining claims (sequence length 256, relatively short token budgets such as 13.1B tokens for 1B, 19.7B for 7B), and there is no wall-clock/compute comparison despite the compute-cost analysis in Table 1, which matters for judging practicality of Muon-class baselines.

Presentation issues reduce polish: multiple typos ('vanila', 'signular-value', 'highly-performed'), inconsistent notation in Theorem 2.1 (∇t_l vs ∇_l), and Figure 3's caption discusses 'different layers' while only two layers are plotted. No explicit code release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility of a method whose value proposition is ease of implementation.

strengths: The paper answers a well-motivated question (what is the minimal modification to SGD needed to match Adam for LLM pretraining?) via a clean, systematic bottom-up study: normalization schemes are first compared in isolation (Table 2), then combined with last-layer momentum (Table 3), with design decisions justified at each step.

The proposed optimizer SCALE is remarkably simple (a few lines on top of SGD), requires essentially no optimizer state beyond vanilla SGD (only last-layer momentum), and the empirical evidence is unusually broad for an optimizer paper: LLaMA 60M–7B at Chinchilla token budgets (Tables 5, 6), additional architectures Qwen2/GPT-2/Gemma-2B (Tables 8, 9), overtraining regimes (Table 10), GLUE fine-tuning (Table 11), throughput comparison (Table 7), and learning-rate sensitivity (Figure 5).

Memory accounting is transparent and reproducible (Appendix A.1 details per-method state sizes; Table 4 summarizes algorithmic components per method), and the paper is honest about which baseline numbers were run by the authors versus copied from prior work (footnotes 5, † marks), and about Fira/APOLLO divergence issues.

The mechanistic investigation is a genuine contribution: Figure 4 shows the last layer has the highest gradient variance, motivating last-layer momentum; Figure 3 and Appendix A.9 (Table 12, Figure 7) give evidence that column-wise (output-dimension) normalization of the LM-head prevents extreme gradient values tied to token frequency, connecting to Kunstner et al. (2024) on the Adam–SGD gap. This goes beyond a purely empirical recipe.

Theorem 2.1 extends the SGD-M analysis of Liu et al. (2020) to a multi-layer setting with layer-wise momentum and variance terms, giving theoretical support for allocating momentum to high-variance layers; the proof (Appendix A.10) appears careful and self-contained.
weaknesses: The theory does not cover the actual algorithm: Theorem 2.1 analyzes plain SGD-M without column-wise normalization, and the authors explicitly decline to analyze Algorithm 1 (page 10). Moreover, the theorem's own implication (f(x) decreasing, so β_l = 1−δ is optimal for all layers) is in tension with the design choice β_l = 0 for non-last layers; the justification relies on a heuristic argument about σ_l ≈ 0 rather than a rigorous trade-off. The theory is thus only loosely suggestive.

Some empirical comparisons are not fully controlled: SWAN results at 60M–350M and APOLLO(-Mini) results at 7B are copied from prior papers rather than rerun under identical settings; SWAN could not be replicated due to code unavailability. No runs appear to be repeated over multiple seeds, and no error bars/variance are reported, which matters given some gaps between methods are small (e.g., SCALE 13.49 vs. APOLLO-Mini 13.48 at 1B).

Ablations are confined to the 130M model (Table 2, Table 12); it remains unverified whether the row-vs-column normalization gap and the variance-based momentum analysis hold at 1B/7B scale, where relative layer parameter fractions shrink.

The explanation for why column-wise normalization matters is partly speculative ('we hypothesize', 'still at a preliminary stage' — Appendix A.9), and the footnote attributing column/row differences to PyTorch tensor strides is vague and unverified.

Presentation issues: several typos and artifacts (e.g., 'σ_l is close to) zero', 'requires significant more memory', 'achieves superior performance than'), a dangling footnote numbering (footnote 2 referenced but missing), and Table 2's normalization ablations confound normalization scheme with the NS approximation only for the singular-value case. The claimed 'matches or exceeds Adam' should be qualified: Stable-SPAM (a stabilized Adam) still outperforms SCALE at 60M and 350M.

strengths: The bottom-up, minimalist methodology is well executed: the paper systematically ablates gradient normalization schemes (Table 2), normalization combined with last-layer momentum (Table 3), and 'mixed' normalization configurations including the last layer (Table 12, A.9), which transparently supports the two design choices behind SCALE.

The empirical evaluation is broad: LLaMA 60M–7B on C4, additional architectures (Qwen2-500M, GPT2-Medium, Gemma-2B), an overtraining regime (Table 10), throughput comparison (Table 7), learning-rate sensitivity (Figure 5), and preliminary fine-tuning results (Table 11).

Memory accounting is careful and reproducible (Appendix A.1), and the paper is honest about caveats: copied SWAN results due to code unavailability, divergence of Fira/APOLLO at default learning rates, and the distinction between memory-efficient and full-memory baselines.

The discussion in A.9 connecting column-wise normalization of the LM-head to token-frequency imbalance in gradient column norms is an interesting, testable hypothesis that goes beyond mere algorithm construction.
Writing is generally clear, and the algorithm is simple enough (Algorithm 1) to be easily implemented and adopted as a baseline.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Both ingredients exist in prior work: column-wise normalization is studied in Scion (Pethick et al., 2025), and the special treatment of the first/last layers is exactly what SWAN does. The contribution is essentially a specific combination plus the observation that momentum is needed only for the LM head; the paper's own 'Connection to existing works' section concedes how close these methods are.

The theory does not cover the proposed method. Theorem 2.1 analyzes SGD-M without column-wise normalization, and the authors explicitly state they 'choose not to present' a convergence analysis of Algorithm 1. Moreover, the remark's own analysis shows f(x) is decreasing, implying the optimal choice is βl = 1−δ for all layers; the memory-saving recommendation (βl = 0 for l < L) rests on the strong, unverified assumption that σl ≈ 0 for all non-last layers, and the variance bound ignores matrix dimensionality.

Statistical rigor is weak: all results appear to be single runs with no error bars, seeds, or variance reporting, and the 1B/7B learning rates are manually tuned (7B uses a single run). Differences between SCALE and Strong baselines such as Stable-SPAM (e.g., 13.49 vs 13.30 at 1B) and Muon at 7B (SCALE only wins at the final step) are within plausible run-to-run noise.

Evaluation is perplexity-only for pretraining; no downstream task evaluation of the pretrained 1B/7B models is provided, which limits evidence that the perplexity gains translate to model quality. The GLUE fine-tuning results are preliminary and only vs. Adam.

Some framing overstates results: the abstract claims SCALE 'matches or exceeds Adam,' yet SCALE trails Adam (Stable-SPAM) at 60M–1B in Table 5, and Figure 1's Pareto-frontier claim depends on memory estimates that exclude activations and gradients and rely on reported numbers from other papers under possibly different settings.

The column- vs row-wise distinction is partially attributed to PyTorch tensor stride layout (footnote 3), raising the concern that a key empirical finding may be implementation-dependent; the paper does not disentangle this from the token-frequency hypothesis, which itself remains speculative.

The momentum hyperparameter is fixed at β = 0.9 with no sensitivity analysis, and the claimed 2× memory advantage over SWAN (13.74G vs 14.52G at 7B) hinges on SWAN using Adam for two layers while SCALE uses Adam only for vector parameters—a comparison whose fairness would benefit from further ablation (e.g., SCALE + Adam on the embedding layer).

strengths: The bottom-up, minimalist methodology is a genuine strength: rather than proposing another complex optimizer, the paper systematically isolates the roles of gradient normalization (Table 2) and selective momentum (Figure 4, Table 3), and the resulting SCALE algorithm is extremely simple with negligible memory overhead (Algorithm 1, Table 4).

Experimental coverage is unusually thorough for this line of work: LLaMA 60M–7B on C4 (Tables 2, 3, 5, 6), additional architectures (Qwen2-500M, GPT2-Medium, Gemma-2B; Tables 8–9), overtraining regimes up to 4x Chinchilla ratio (Table 10), throughput analysis (Table 7), fine-tuning (Table 11), and learning-rate sensitivity (Figure 5).

The memory accounting is transparent (Appendix A.1), and the authors are candid about copying baseline results where replication was impossible (footnotes 5, Table 6), about learning-rate tuning for diverging baselines, and about the scope of the method (Section A.6).

The analysis of why the last layer matters—high gradient variance (Figure 4), token-frequency-driven column-norm imbalance (Figure 7, Appendix A.9), and the mixed-normalization ablations (Table 12)—provides a plausible and interesting mechanistic explanation connecting to Kunstner et al. (2024).
The method sits on the memory/perplexity Pareto frontier (Figure 1) and achieves strong results even at 7B (Table 6), suggesting the finding is not an artifact of small-scale experiments.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest: both ingredients are individually well-known. Column-wise normalization appears in Scion (Pethick et al., 2025) and 'Adam for the last layer' is standard in GaLore/Fira/APOLLO/SWAN; the contribution is essentially the combination plus the ablation study. The paper acknowledges these connections but the delta over Scion-like methods is not sharply delineated experimentally.

There is a theory–algorithm gap. Theorem 2.1 analyzes plain per-layer-momentum SGD-M (2.7), not SCALE (which uses column-wise normalization), and the authors explicitly decline to provide a convergence guarantee for Algorithm 1 (Section 3). The theorem's practical message (assign momentum to high-variance layers) is qualitative; the derivation that β_l = 1−δ is optimal but β_l = 0 is 'fine' for near-zero variance is loose and does not quantitatively justify the specific design.

Several headline comparisons are fragile: (a) the 60M–350M Adam/Adam-Stable-SPAM/GaLore/Fira numbers are taken from Glentis et al. (2025) rather than rerun; (b) the 7B APOLLO numbers are copied from Zhu et al. (2025) under potentially different hardware/settings; (c) the 7B SCALE and Muon results are single runs with no seed variance reported, while the margins are small (12.59 vs 12.72); (d) perplexity differences at 1B (13.49 vs 13.48 for APOLLO-Mini) are within noise for single-run experiments.

The memory-savings comparison is partially advantaged by the design of baselines: GaLore/Fira/APOLLO/SWAN keep full Adam on the first and last layers, which dominates on small models. A fairer comparison would also try applying SCALE-style last-layer-only treatment to those baselines, since the '59% of the memory cost' claim depends on this design choice. Reported memory also excludes gradients and activations, so the practical end-to-end savings are smaller than the optimizer-state numbers suggest.

The proof in Appendix A.10 contains notational errors (e.g., in (A.10) the factor c_{l,1} is incorrectly pulled inside the sum defining m_t^l, and Lemma A.3's proof contains typos such as z_2 − z_1 written as z_1^2 − z_1^1), which undermines confidence in the extension's correctness even if the argument is broadly a re-derivation of Liu et al. (2020).

Throughput of the key ablation methods (column-wise normalization cost) is presented for standalone normalization ops (Table 1) but the end-to-end throughput for intermediate ablation configurations is not reported, and hyperparameter sensitivity beyond the learning rate (e.g., the momentum β=0.9 choice for the last layer) is not ablated.
